lessons.title: How Banks Make Money: NIM, CASA, and the Cost of Funds

body.text: A bank is a spread business. It borrows money from depositors, lends it out at a higher rate, and keeps the difference. The banks that win over decades are rarely the ones that lend at the highest rates. They are the ones that borrow most cheaply, and that advantage starts with your salary account.

children.text: Financial services is the largest sector in the Nifty 50, so understanding banks is not optional for an Indian investor. It is also the sector where the usual analysis habits break down most. Revenue growth, operating margin, and debt to equity all mean something different here. This chapter rebuilds your toolkit for financials, starting with the engine room: where a bank's income comes from and what it costs to earn it.
The Bank Business Model in One Picture

On the liability side, a bank raises money mainly through deposits, plus some borrowings and its own equity. On the asset side, it lends most of that money as loans, known in Indian bank filings as advances, and parks a meaningful share in government securities, partly because the RBI requires it through the Statutory Liquidity Ratio. A slice is kept as cash with the RBI under the Cash Reserve Ratio, which earns no interest. The bank earns interest on loans and investments, pays interest on deposits and borrowings, collects fees for services, pays for branches and staff, and sets aside provisions for loans that may go bad.

body.text: On Screener.in, a bank's 'Revenue' is mostly interest income and its 'Interest' line is interest paid to depositors, not a financing cost to be minimised like in a manufacturing company. Do not read a bank's revenue growth or interest burden the way you would for an FMCG or cement company.

children.text: NIM: The Single Most Watched Bank Number

body.latex: \text{NIM} = \frac{\text{Interest earned} - \text{Interest expended}}{\text{Average interest-earning assets}} = \frac{\text{NII}}{\text{Average interest-earning assets}}
body.caption: Net Interest Margin (NIM). Banks usually report it as an annualised percentage every quarter.

children.text: NIM tells you how much a bank earns on every ₹100 of assets that generate interest, after paying for the money it borrowed. Two forces set it: the yield the bank earns on advances and investments, and the cost of funds it pays to depositors and lenders. A bank can raise NIM by lending to higher-yield segments such as credit cards, personal loans, and small business loans, or by lowering its cost of funds. The first route usually brings more risk. The second is the durable one.

body.title: Calculate the NIM
body.prompt: Using the illustrative bank above, with Net Interest Income of ₹4,600 crore and interest-earning assets of ₹1,20,000 crore, what is its NIM? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: NIM = ₹4,600 crore ÷ ₹1,20,000 crore = 3.83%. For context, large Indian private sector banks have typically reported NIMs in roughly the 3.5% to 4.5% range, while public sector banks have usually been lower, around 3%. Small differences matter: 0.25 percentage points on ₹1,20,000 crore of assets is ₹300 crore of annual income.

children.text: CASA: Why Cheap Deposits Are a Moat

markDefs.definition: Current Account and Savings Account deposits as a percentage of total deposits. Current accounts pay no interest and savings accounts pay low interest, so a higher CASA ratio means a cheaper funding base.

children.text: Deposits come in three flavours. Current accounts, used by businesses for daily transactions, pay zero interest. Savings accounts pay a low rate, often in the 2.5% to 3% range at large banks. Term deposits, the fixed deposits retail investors love, pay much more. The share of the first two in total deposits is the

. Customers do not keep money in a current or savings account for the interest. They keep it there for convenience: salary credits, UPI payments, business collections, a nearby branch. That habit is hard for a competitor to steal, which is why a high CASA ratio is one of the strongest competitive advantages in banking.

body.title: What a Weaker Deposit Franchise Costs
body.prompt: Using the comparison above, how much more does Bank Y pay in deposit interest each year than Bank X, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹5,800 crore - ₹5,025 crore = ₹775 crore a year, a gap of about 0.78 percentage points in cost of deposits. To earn the same NIM, Bank Y must lend at higher rates, which usually means taking on riskier borrowers. Or it accepts lower profitability. Either way, the deposit franchise shows up in the numbers every single year.

children.text: Fees and Efficiency: The Other Two Levers

Beyond interest, banks earn other income. The high-quality part is fee income: credit card fees, loan processing charges, commissions from selling insurance and mutual funds, and transaction banking. The volatile part is treasury income, gains from trading government bonds, which rises when bond yields fall and can turn into losses when yields rise. When a bank's profit jumps because of treasury gains, discount it. On the cost side, the key ratio is cost to income.

body.caption: Lower is more efficient. A bank investing heavily in new branches will temporarily show a higher ratio.

The average interest rate a bank earns on its loan book.
The average interest rate a bank pays across deposits and borrowings.
Pre-Provision Operating Profit: net interest income plus other income minus operating expenses, before provisions for bad loans. Shows core earning power.
Advances divided by deposits. A high ratio means the bank has lent out most of its deposits and may need to raise deposits faster or rely on costlier borrowings.
Statutory Liquidity Ratio: the share of deposits a bank must hold in liquid assets, mainly government securities. Money held here earns a lower yield than loans.
Cash Reserve Ratio: the share of deposits a bank must keep as cash with the RBI. It earns no interest, so it directly reduces NIM.

body.title: What Really Drives a Durable NIM?
body.question: Two private banks both report a NIM of 4.2%. Which additional fact suggests Bank A's margin is more durable than Bank B's?
options: Bank A has grown its credit card and unsecured personal loan book much faster than Bank B
Bank A has a CASA ratio of 45% while Bank B's is 28%
Bank A booked large treasury gains this year
Bank A's loan book grew 30% in a year while Bank B's grew 15%
body.explanation: A higher CASA ratio means Bank A earns its margin through cheap, sticky funding rather than risky lending. Bank B likely needs higher-yield loans to reach the same NIM. Fast growth in unsecured loans can inflate NIM temporarily while raising credit risk, treasury gains affect other income rather than NIM, and rapid loan growth on its own says nothing about margin quality.

body.title: Indian context: the deposit squeeze of 2023 to 2024

children.text: After the RBI's 2022 to 2023 rate hikes, loan demand in India stayed strong, but deposit growth lagged behind loan growth across the system. Savers also shifted money from low-yield savings accounts into higher-paying fixed deposits, so CASA ratios fell at many banks. Banks competed for deposits by raising FD rates, which pushed up their cost of funds and squeezed NIMs even as loan rates stayed high. Credit-deposit ratios climbed, and the RBI publicly flagged the gap between credit and deposit growth. HDFC Bank's merger with its parent HDFC Ltd in July 2023 was a prominent example: the merged bank took on a large mortgage book funded largely by borrowings rather than deposits, lifting its credit-deposit ratio and making deposit mobilisation a stated priority. The episode showed that in banking, the liability side often decides the growth rate.

body.title: When FD Rates Start Rising
body.scenario: Fixed deposit rates across the banking system are rising because deposit growth is lagging loan growth. You hold two bank stocks. Bank P has a CASA ratio of 45%, a credit-deposit ratio of 78%, and grows its loan book at 14% a year. Bank Q has a CASA ratio of 30%, a credit-deposit ratio of 96%, and grows its loan book at 24% a year, faster than its deposits.
body.prompt: Which bank's NIM is more at risk over the next few quarters, and why? What would you look for in the next investor presentation?
body.modelAnswer: Bank Q is more exposed. With only 30% CASA, a larger share of its deposits are term deposits that reprice upward as FD rates rise. A 96% credit-deposit ratio means it has lent out almost all its deposits, so to keep growing at 24% it must either raise deposits aggressively by offering higher FD rates or rely on costlier market borrowings. Both push up its cost of funds and compress NIM. Bank P has cheaper, stickier funding and room to grow without chasing deposits. In the next investor presentation, check: cost of funds or cost of deposits trend, CASA ratio movement, deposit growth versus loan growth, the credit-deposit ratio, NIM guidance, and any sign of loan growth being slowed deliberately to protect margins.

body.explanation: Current accounts pay nothing and savings accounts pay little, so a high CASA ratio gives a bank a structural funding cost advantage.

body.title: Reading the Earnings Engine in a Bank's Quarterly Investor Presentation
steps: Find the NIM for the quarter and compare it with the previous four quarters, not just the same quarter last year
Note yield on advances and cost of funds separately to see which one moved the NIM
Check the CASA ratio trend and whether deposit growth is keeping up with advances growth
Calculate or find the credit-deposit ratio and note if it is rising toward or above 90%
Split other income into fees and treasury gains, and mentally strip out treasury gains
Note the cost-to-income ratio and what management says about branch expansion or technology spend
Compare all of the above with two or three peers of similar size and ownership, private with private and public with public

points: A bank earns the spread between what it charges borrowers and what it pays depositors, plus fees, minus operating costs and provisions
Net Interest Margin (NIM) = Net Interest Income ÷ average interest-earning assets, and is the most watched measure of a bank's core profitability
CASA deposits are cheap and sticky; a high CASA ratio lowers the cost of funds and is one of the strongest moats in banking
Fee income is high quality; treasury income swings with bond yields and should be discounted
Cost-to-income ratio measures efficiency; lower is better, but temporary spikes can reflect investment in growth
When deposit growth lags loan growth, banks with low CASA and high credit-deposit ratios face the sharpest margin pressure
